name: Fever Ray
label: Rabid Records / Mute
lede: Karin Dreijer fronted a Gothenburg guitar band, then The Knife with brother Olof, then stepped out alone in a mask, and in 2023 made an album about love that Pitchfork put at No. 8 for the year.

eras.title: A Gothenburg indie band, then a brother
eras.text: Karin Dreijer starts out fronting Honey Is Cool, a guitar band that ends in July 2000. The next project is a synth duo with brother Olof Dreijer, and it inherits the label.

years.src: Wikipedia: Honey Is Cool · Wikipedia: Karin Dreijer
years.h: Honey Is Cool starts in Gothenburg with Karin Dreijer up front
years.p: Dreijer, born April 7, 1975, picked up guitar at ten and fronts the band for its whole run, with John Jern, Staffan Larsson, Tina Weibull and Fredrik Wennerlund in the final line-up.
years.xp:
Wikipedia describes Dreijer as the band's frontperson and main creative force from 1994 to 2000, and says they moved to Stockholm in 1998. Honey Is Cool went from Sunspot to MVG and then to a label of their own.

The band's name for that label was Rabid Records. Wikipedia's Honey Is Cool page credits the band with setting it up; its Knife page credits the duo. Either way, Rabid outlived both.

years.h: Crazy Love: Honey Is Cool's debut album on MVG
years.p: Dreijer's first album is a band record, guitars and keyboards, a long way from the pitch-shifted voice that comes later.

years.h: Early Morning Are You Working? is the band's last album
years.p: The second and final Honey Is Cool album comes out a year before the split. [[The Knife|bf710b71-48e5-4e15-9bd6-96debb2e4e98]] is already in motion in Gothenburg.

years.src: Wikipedia: Honey Is Cool · Wikipedia: The Knife
years.h: Honey Is Cool calls it quits on July 3
years.p: Wikipedia says the split came because Dreijer wanted to focus on a new project and drummer Fredrik Wennerlund had other plans.
years.xp: The new project was The Knife, formed with Olof Dreijer in Gothenburg in 1999. Wikipedia notes that ideas from Honey Is Cool songs resurface on The Knife's 2003 album Deep Cuts.

eras.title: Two siblings, a label, and an ad they didn't plan
eras.text: The Knife's first two albums on Rabid put Karin and Olof Dreijer on the map, and a Swedish folk singer's cover of one song puts their music on TV screens worldwide.

years.h: The Knife: the siblings' self-titled debut on Rabid
years.p: A synth-pop debut from Karin and Olof Dreijer, released on the label the family already ran themselves.

years.h: Deep Cuts: a Swedish breakout with "Heartbeats" on it
years.p: Rabid puts out the second Knife album on January 17. Pitchfork gave it 7.6, and Mute issued it in the US on October 31, 2006.
years.xp: The singles were "Heartbeats" (December 27, 2002), "You Take My Breath Away" (March 28, 2003) and "Pass This On" (June 13, 2005), per Wikipedia. Swedish magazine Sonic later put the album at No. 4 on its list of the 100 best Swedish albums ever.

years.h: The Knife win a Grammis and send Guerrilla Girls to collect it
years.p: Wikipedia says the duo boycotted the Swedish ceremony after winning Pop Group of the Year, sending Guerrilla Girls representatives wearing the number 50 instead.
years.xp: The protest was aimed at male dominance in the music industry, per Wikipedia. The Knife skipped later Grammis ceremonies too, sometimes sending manipulated videos, and kept to beaked Venetian-style masks in promo photos.

years.h: A bouncing-ball ad turns a Knife song into someone else's hit
years.p: Sony's Bravia commercial used José González's acoustic cover of "Heartbeats", which Wikipedia says did better than The Knife's original and reached No. 9 in the UK.
years.xp: According to Wikipedia, the duo defended taking the money by saying they needed it to fund Rabid Records, despite their anti-commercial stance. Wikipedia's two pages disagree on whether the ad ran in 2005 or 2006; the song page says November 2005.

eras.title: Masks on, lights out
eras.text: Silent Shout turns the siblings from a studio project into a stage act, and Karin's solo work starts in earnest.

years.h: Silent Shout arrives: cold synths, a voice pitched into a monster
years.p: Recorded in Stockholm between March 2004 and November 2005, it hits No. 1 in Sweden. Wikipedia says Pitchfork named it the best album of 2006.
years.xp: Karin Dreijer's pitch-shifted, multi-tracked vocals are the sound everyone remembers, and the album's singles were "Silent Shout," "Marble House," "We Share Our Mothers' Health" and "Like a Pen." Pitchfork later ranked the title track at No. 74 on its list of the 2000s' top tracks and the album 15th among the decade's best.

years.cap: Fever Ray performing at Terminal 5 · Wikimedia
years.h: First-ever live shows: the Silent Shout tour
years.p: Wikipedia says The Knife's first live performances came only in 2006, after seven years as a studio duo.

years.src: Wikipedia: Karin Dreijer · Wikipedia: The Knife
years.h: "If I Had a Heart" is the first Fever Ray single
years.p: Dreijer's solo song came out under a new name in 2008, and later showed up in Breaking Bad, Horns and as the theme for Vikings.
years.xp: Wikipedia lists appearances in Person of Interest, Breaking Bad, Wentworth and Laurence Anyways as well. Dreijer had also guested with [[Röyksopp|1c70a3fc-fa3c-4be1-8b55-c3192db8a884]] on "What Else Is There?" in 2005 and on their Junior tracks in 2009.

eras.title: Fever Ray, a Darwin opera, and Coachella
eras.text: Dreijer puts out a first solo album under the name Fever Ray while The Knife is working on a Darwin opera with Mt. Sims and Planningtorock.

years.src: Wikipedia: Fever Ray (2009 album) · Wikipedia: Karin Dreijer
years.h: Fever Ray: a solo album made in a colder room
years.p: Digital release January 12, physical on March 18; Pitchfork gave it 8.1 and placed it 9th on its 2009 year-end list.
years.xp: Wikipedia says The Guardian named it the second-best album of 2009, and The Observer called it "an astonishingly stark record." AllMusic compared its isolation to Björk's Homogenic. Singles: "If I Had a Heart," "When I Grow Up," "Triangle Walks" and "Seven."

years.h: Coachella and Electric Picnic: the Fever Ray costumes go on tour
years.p: Wikipedia says Dreijer's 2010 Coachella set drew positive reviews, and the live show used masks, body paint and gauze screens.
years.xp: The Electric Picnic set in Ireland followed that September. Wikipedia describes Dreijer's live look as theatrical costumes, masks and body paint with gauze screens in front.

years.h: Tomorrow, in a Year: The Knife write an opera about Darwin
years.p: With Mt. Sims and Planningtorock, the duo scored Hotel Pro Forma's stage piece on On the Origin of Species; Pitchfork gave the 92-minute album 6.9.
years.xp: Wikipedia says it was recorded in Berlin, Stockholm and Copenhagen during 2008-2009 and marks Darwin's 150th anniversary. Drowned in Sound gave it 10/10; BBC Music called it "complicated, esoteric and, yes, really quite bonkers." Wikipedia's page gives February 1 as the release date while The Knife's page says March 1, so it is dated to the year here.

years.h: Dreijer scores Hour of the Wolf for the stage
years.p: Wikipedia lists music for the theatre piece in 2011 and for Vahák in 2016, alongside the Fever Ray and Knife records.

eras.title: A political record, then the last show
eras.text: The Knife's fourth album is their most argued-over, and they end it on their own terms.

q: That should be impossible to misunderstand.
years.h: Shaking the Habitual: three LPs of politics and noise
years.p: Rabid released it in April with a title borrowed from Foucault, per Wikipedia. Pitchfork gave it 8.4 and called it the duo's "most political, ambitious, accomplished album."
years.xp:
The Dreijers say it draws on feminist and queer theory, environmentalism and structuralism, and criticizes wealth inequality and the nuclear family. Shannon Funchess of [[Light Asylum|a077a16e-edb1-43b2-99a4-460cab3b6a6e]] sings on "Stay Out Here," with lyrics by artist Emily Roysdon, and Liv Strömquist's comic "End Extreme Wealth" is the artwork.

It reached No. 52 on the Billboard 200 and won the Nordic Music Prize in March 2014, per Wikipedia. Lead single "Full of Fire" came with a short film by Marit Östberg.

years.cap: Fever Ray en concert au festival Rock en Seine le 25 août 2023. · Wikimedia
years.h: Last show: "Post-Colonial Gender Politics Come First, Music Comes Second"
years.p: The Knife announced they were done on August 21, then played their farewell at Iceland Airwaves, released afterward as a film and special-edition vinyl.
years.xp: Wikipedia dates the announcement to August 21, 2014 and the Reykjavik show to November 8. The show's title is what The Knife called the tour's final performance.

eras.title: Plunge: a fast, physical second act
eras.text: After eight years Fever Ray comes back with a record built by club producers and aimed at the body.

years.h: Plunge: Fever Ray's comeback lands a week after its single
years.p: "To the Moon and Back" came out October 20, the album October 27. Metacritic scored it 87, and Pitchfork's Philip Sherburne called it "thrillingly restless."
years.xp: Wikipedia lists Paula Temple, Deena Abdelwahed, Nídia, Tami T, [[Peder Mannerfelt|4f9f50e9-7962-4792-86f6-cb5452d937f6]] and Johannes Berglund among the producers, with more direct political and sexual themes than the 2009 debut. "Wanna Sip" (January 23, 2018) and "IDK About You" (March 1, 2018) followed.

years.h: The Plunge tour runs Europe from February and North America in May
years.p: Wikipedia also says Dreijer's team won Producer of the Year at the 2018 Swedish Grammis.
years.xp: Wikipedia says Plunge was also nominated for IMPALA's Best European Independent Album.

years.big: "Music works for me as a totally open space."
years.src: NPR: Fever Ray · Wikipedia: Karin Dreijer
years.h: Dreijer starts using they/them and hen
years.p: Wikipedia says Karin Dreijer began using they/them in English and hen in Swedish in 2019; NPR quotes the line above from their 2023 interviews.
years.xp: Wikipedia says they identify as queer and gender-fluid. NPR's review of Radical Romantics quotes Dreijer saying they do not have to think about gender so much in music.

years.h: Country Creatures: Björk and Fever Ray swap remixes
years.p: Each remixes a track from the other's 2017 album (Plunge and Björk's Utopia), and The Knife add a third remix even though they split in 2014.
years.xp: Wikipedia says the three remixes came out digitally September 6, 2019 and on a One Little Indian 12-inch on November 1.

eras.title: Radical Romantics
eras.text: Fever Ray's third album is a record about love, and Pitchfork counts it among the year's best.

years.h: "What They Call Us" is the first single
years.p: It comes in October 2022 and is followed by "Carbon Dioxide" in November.

years.h: "Kandy" is the third single
years.p: The video arrives ahead of the March 10 album. Director Martin Falck shared behind-the-scenes photos with PAPER.

years.src: Album of the Year · Wikipedia: Radical Romantics · NPR: Fever Ray
years.h: Radical Romantics: Pitchfork gives it 8.4 and ranks it No. 8 of 2023
years.p: Anna Gaca's Pitchfork review scores it 8.4; the album also made Pitchfork's year-end top 50 at No. 8. Rabid and Mute put it out on March 10.
years.xp:
Wikipedia and Album of the Year both report Pitchfork's score as 8.4 (84), with Gaca writing that the record renders "the search for love as something both sensual and alien." Uncut gave it 8.7. Not everyone bit: Slant asked where an artist this singular goes from here, and The Arts Desk said it "sounds exactly like a Fever Ray album."

Karin Dreijer co-produced with Olof Dreijer, with Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, Vessel, Nídia, Pär Grindvik, Peder Mannerfelt and Aasthma. Johannes Berglund handled vocal production, per Wikipedia and NPR. It ranked 28th in The Wire's year-end poll.

years.h: The Year of the Radical Romantics is the live album
years.p: A retrospective that pairs tracks from Radical Romantics and Plunge with reworked older songs from the tour.
